p: It is a curious fact that the longest period in the history of mankind is named after a material, and that the material is stone. The antiquaries of Denmark, who were obliged earlier in this century to arrange the contents of their national museum, divided the past into an Age of Stone, an Age of Bronze and an Age of Iron. The scheme was the work chiefly of Mr Christian Jürgensen Thomsen of Copenhagen, and it was so convenient that all Europe adopted it. It has the merit of naming each age after the thing which survives from it. Wood rots, leather perishes, songs are forgotten; stone remains. We know the Stone Age chiefly through its rubbish.

The Encyclopaedia of the future tells me that the oldest known stone tools are now thought to be about three million three hundred thousand years old, found at a place in Kenya called Lomekwi, beside Lake Turkana. They are older than any bones yet found of our own genus, which means either that they were made by one of the older ape-like ancestors, or that our genus is older than its bones have yet confessed. Somewhat younger, about two million six hundred thousand years old, are the tools of the kind the learned call Oldowan, after the Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, where a family of diggers named Leakey spent much of the twentieth century on their knees.
## How a stone becomes a tool

An Oldowan tool is easily described and not easily made. One takes a rounded pebble of a suitable stone, such as flint or quartz or volcanic glass, and strikes it with another stone, so that a sharp flake springs away. The flake itself is a knife; the pebble, with its new jagged edge, is a chopper. Anyone who has tried this, as I once did on a holiday in Norfolk, to the great amusement of a shepherd, will know that it requires a precise blow at a precise angle, and that the stone does not forgive carelessness. To make such a tool is to understand, at least in the hands, the hidden properties of a material. It is the beginning of engineering.

With such edges our ancestors could cut meat from the carcass of an animal, break open bones for the marrow, and shape wood. It is very likely that they used them first upon the leavings of lions and other hunters, for a creature with a sharp flake may take what a creature with only teeth must leave. The Encyclopaedia reports that bones bearing the marks of stone cutting are found from very early times. I do not find it undignified that our first trade was scavenging. Many a noble house was founded on less.

About one million seven hundred thousand years ago appeared a more ambitious instrument: the hand-axe, of the kind called Acheulean, after the village of Saint-Acheul in northern France where they were found in great numbers. The name is French, but needs no translating; it is simply the name of a place. A hand-axe is shaped on both faces into a pointed oval, rather like a large almond or a pear, and often with a symmetry that is not strictly necessary for cutting. It is the most successful tool design in the history of the world. It was made, with only modest changes, for well over a million years, across Africa, Europe and much of Asia.

I wish you to consider that figure. A million years. The whole of recorded history could be repeated two hundred times within the life of the hand-axe. Our modern manufacturers boast if a pattern of locomotive lasts twenty years. There is something in this extraordinary steadiness that ought to give a historian pause. Either the minds that made these tools were, for all their skill, much less given to novelty than ours, or the hand-axe was so nearly perfect for its purposes that there was little reason to change it. I suspect both.

The symmetry of the better hand-axes has suggested to some scholars that they were made with an eye to beauty as well as use, and that a fine axe may have been something to admire, or to give, or even to display before a prospective husband or wife. I report the opinion without endorsing it. It is the sort of theory that tells us as much about the theorist as about the past. Yet it is true that some hand-axes are larger than any reasonable use would require, and some are made from beautiful stones, and some were apparently never used at all.

Later, from around three hundred thousand years ago, the makers of tools learned to prepare a core of stone so that a single blow would strike off a flake of a shape decided in advance. The technique is named after a suburb of Paris, Levallois, and it requires the craftsman to think several steps ahead, as a chess player does. The Neanderthals were masters of it. Later still, our own species made long, slender blades, and tiny pointed pieces called microliths, which could be set in rows into handles of wood or bone with natural glues of resin and tar. By then a tool was no longer a single stone, but an assembly of several materials, prepared by several processes. When a man must cook birch bark to make glue to fix a stone point to a wooden shaft to make a spear, he is no longer merely handy. He is a manufacturer.

The study of these tools is the study of minds that left no other record. A sequence of blows struck in a particular order shows foresight. A tool made from a stone carried many miles shows either travel or trade. A tool workshop where the same patterns are made generation after generation shows teaching, for no child discovers the Levallois method alone. Wherever the stones show us a tradition, they show us a society that passed knowledge from the old to the young, which is, after all, the whole of civilisation in its simplest form.

The Age of Stone did not end everywhere at once, and in some places it has not ended in my own lifetime. The peoples of Tasmania, whose dreadful fate at the hands of my own countrymen I shall not dwell upon here, lived by stone tools within living memory. So let us not imagine the Stone Age as a dim and finished thing. It is the foundation on which everything else is built, and it lasted, by any honest reckoning, for more than ninety-nine parts in every hundred of the human story.
